newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Changes to NZ framework unlikely, S&P says again.
newsitem.headline: Changes to NZ framework unlikely, S&P says again.

text.p: Standard & Poor's on Friday repeated earlier comments that changes to the major planks of New Zealand's economic framework were relatively unlikely despite the outcome of next week's eleciton.

S&P Sovereign Risk Managing Director David Beers told Radio New Zealand that he agreed that it would be a "worrisome development" if there were a change of government and there were changes to the Reserve Bank Act, labour market legislation, buy-backs of former state assets and limits imposed on foreign investment.
"From our standpoint that seems to be relatively unlikely," he said.
The RNZ interviewer noted that the left-wing Alliance, which may hold the balance of power after the October 12 election, favours all of the changes that Beers said would concern him.
Beers replied: "Holding the balance of power in a dynamic situation operating under new voting rules isn't necessarily the same thing as getting your way on everything. That's the point."
S&P had taken all possibilities into account because it believed that under the new electoral rules governments in the future would be pulled towards centrist economic positions.
Beers said S&P was well aware of the position of the parties and also well aware that the parties disagree, in some cases fundamentally on key aspects of economic policy going forward.
He said there was a lot of certainty in the run up to this election but S&P had had much experience rating countries with similar types of electoral systems.

"What we find is when the smoke clears and governments are put together they tend to adopt and continue with centrist type of economic policies," he said, adding that the New Zealand's economy was as sound as it had been in many years.
Prime Minister Jim Bolger crossed swords with S&P on Thursday when he warned of job cuts, capital flight and higher inflation if the left won power at next week's general election.
He referred to earlier comments by Beers that drastic policy changes were unlikely and New Zealand's AA+ rating was not threatened by the election.
Bolger said it would be extraordinary if a change in policy direction did not affect the rating, a key measure of the country's creditworthiness.
"If Standard & Poor's wants to come out and say 'that's fine by them', well let them do it, but I have to say I think that would be totally wrong," Bolger said.
